Dealer Uncovers 1957 Ford Thunderbird That Spent Decades in a Heated Garage, Not All Good News
42 photos
Photo: Imports & Classics on eBay
Locked in heated storage. That’s pretty much all you need to know about this Ford Thunderbird if you’re trying to figure out its condition. The car looks great, considering it doesn’t boast a recent restoration, and the only urgent work it needs is under the hood.
The dealer responsible for finding a new home for this T-Bird says it loud and clear: this car needs to be gone through to get to safe, running condition.
A full restoration doesn’t seem to be required, considering the overall shape, but asking your mechanic to open the hood and inspect everything in there is obviously recommended.
Photo: Imports & Classics on eBay The battle for the number one spot in the American car space was getting fiercer in 1957. With Chevrolet launching a new Bel Air, whose new major selling point was the 283 Turbo-Fire, Ford also needed to focus more on engine power. This is why an upgraded version of a 312 ended up seeing the rollout in 1957. The supercharged engine produced no more, no less than 300 horsepower.
The base Thunderbird continued to be offered with a 292, while the 312 was offered as an option with three power configurations, namely 245, 270, and 285 horsepower. In terms of transmissions, Thunderbird buyers could choose between 3-speed manuals, overdrives, and the famous Ford-O-Matic automatic.
Ford’s strategy worked, as the company secured the leading spot for another year before losing it in 1958 when the Impala came out. Ford ended the year with 21,380 T-Birds rolling off the assembly lines, with 1957, therefore, becoming the most successful year of this nameplate until that point.
The Thunderbird was slated to get bigger changes in the following years, with a larger model planned for 1958. However, the battle in this space was getting fiercer, especially as General Motors started focusing more on full-size cars with a completely redesigned lineup planned for the 1958 model year .
Photo: Imports & Classics on eBay This particular Thunderbird is fitted with a 292 engine paired with a Ford-O-Matic transmission. We’re not getting any insights into this engine’s past, but it’s safe to assume that this is the original configuration.
As the dealer explains, the engine turns over but does not currently run. However, considering it’s been sitting in a heated garage, bringing it back to life should be totally doable, especially considering that the engine was running prior to being parked.
I would still ask my mechanic to go there in person and check the engine in person, as retaining the original engine, even if it’s the base setup, should be a priority for every buyer.
Still fitted with the removable factory hardtop, this Thunderbird looks to be in good shape, and you can tell it’s been stored in the right conditions. The non-running engine is probably a victim of the car not being regularly started, but otherwise, the rust clearly hasn’t taken its toll on this Thunderbird.
Photo: Imports & Classics on eBay If you’re particularly interested in the mileage, this is where things get tricky. While the car has been parked for 20 years, so you’d normally expect it to be a low-mile specimen, the true mileage is actually unknown.
The odometer shows 13,122 miles, which would be a fantastic number for a 1957 car, but the actual mileage isn’t known at this point.
It’s difficult how original and complete the car continues to be after all these years, but the seller reveals that the T-Bird needs new tires, but comes with an original-style dashboard.
Photo: Imports & Classics on eBay This Thunderbird is undoubtedly an intriguing presence, especially thanks to its condition. But without answers to the big questions, including regarding the previous ownership and the work this car has already received, it’s hard to think that it would just sell overnight.
An in-person inspection and more details offered by the dealer are must-haves, so contact them with all your questions if you’re interested in a purchase.
Otherwise, just be ready to pay $26,000 for this car. The dealer believes this is a fair price, but the Make Offer option has also been enabled, so with the right negotiation skills, you might be able to get a better deal. I wouldn’t expect the price to drop significantly though, so maybe $25,000 is the best deal you could get.
Meanwhile, the vehicle is parked in Bellingham, Washington, and considering the engine is no longer running, you should also find transportation. This could be a problem for someone living far from this location, as the final cost of the acquisition would increase significantly.
The listing is set to expire in 7 days, so theoretically, you have enough time to convince your significant other, call the dealer, get all the information you need, and then go there in person to see the Thunderbird with your own eyes. Make sure you also ask about the documentation that could be available with this car, including the build sheet.
Via // eBay
